name: Data protection profile (GDPR & DPA)
description: A detailed profile of how this AI system handles personal data. Based on your answers we show which GDPR and Data Processing Agreement obligations apply, the specific thresholds and figures involved, where each rule does NOT apply, and what to do.
penaltiesNote: Infringements can be fined up to €20 million or 4% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher (GDPR Art. 83(5)); lesser breaches up to €10 million or 2% (Art. 83(4)).

questions.prompt: Does the system process any personal data (names, emails, IDs, location, behaviour, photos, etc.)?
questions.helpText: If it never touches personal data, most of the GDPR does not apply.

questions.prompt: Roughly how many people's data does it process?
questions.helpText: Scale drives whether processing is 'large-scale' for DPIA and DPO purposes.

questions.prompt: Which sensitive categories of data does it process, if any?
questions.helpText: Health, biometric, genetic, racial/ethnic, religious, political, sexual, trade-union are 'special category' (Art. 9). Criminal-offence data is Art. 10.

questions.prompt: Is the personal data pseudonymised (direct identifiers replaced with keys) where possible?
questions.helpText: Pseudonymisation is a recognised safeguard, though the data is still personal data.

questions.prompt: Does it process the personal data of children?
questions.helpText: In Germany the digital age of consent is 16 (GDPR Art. 8 allows 13–16; Germany kept 16).

questions.prompt: How large is your organisation?
questions.helpText: The 250-employee mark matters for the records exemption (Art. 30(5) GDPR). Under the EU AI Act, a company that is not an SME, has fewer than 750 staff and turnover up to EUR 150 million (or a balance sheet up to EUR 129 million) is a small mid-cap and gets some of the SME simplifications.

questions.prompt: How many of your staff are constantly engaged in the automated processing of personal data?
questions.helpText: Germany (§38 BDSG) requires a Data Protection Officer once 20 or more people are.

questions.prompt: Do you process this data on behalf of another organisation (you are a processor, not the controller)?
questions.helpText: A processor follows the controller's instructions and has its own duties.

questions.prompt: Do you decide the purposes and means of processing jointly with another organisation?
questions.helpText: Two organisations deciding together are joint controllers (Art. 26).

questions.prompt: Is your organisation established outside the EU/EEA while offering this service to people in the EU?
questions.helpText: Non-EU controllers offering to EU users must appoint an EU representative (Art. 27).

questions.prompt: Which lawful basis do you rely on for this processing?
questions.helpText: Each Art. 6 basis carries different duties.

questions.prompt: Do you use the data for direct marketing or advertising profiling?
questions.helpText: Marketing triggers an absolute right to object (Art. 21) and German ePrivacy rules (TDDDG).

questions.prompt: Does it make automated decisions with a legal or similarly significant effect on people (e.g. credit, hiring, benefits)?
questions.helpText: Decisions made without meaningful human involvement trigger Art. 22.

questions.prompt: Do you use a third-party vendor or cloud/AI provider to process the data (e.g. AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, OpenAI)?
questions.helpText: Anyone processing the data on your behalf is a 'processor'.

questions.prompt: Do you have a signed Data Processing Agreement (Art. 28) with each of those processors?
questions.helpText: A DPA is the contract that lets a processor handle personal data for you lawfully.

questions.prompt: Does each Data Processing Agreement (AVV) cover all the required Art. 28(3) clauses — documented instructions, confidentiality, security, sub-processor approval, assistance with data-subject requests and breaches, audit rights, and deletion or return of the data at the end?
questions.helpText: A signed AVV only counts if it contains the eight Art. 28(3) points. Consumer AI tiers rarely include a complete AVV; business/enterprise tiers bind the standard AVV automatically.

questions.prompt: Do those processors use their own sub-processors (e.g. the AI vendor runs on another company's cloud)?
questions.helpText: Sub-processors must be authorised and flowed-down the same obligations (Art. 28(2),(4)).

questions.prompt: Have you approved each sub-processor in writing and made sure your processor flows down the same Art. 28 obligations to them?
questions.helpText: Under Art. 28(2),(4) sub-processors need your prior authorisation and must be bound to the same data-protection terms; your processor stays fully liable for them.

questions.prompt: Is your AI provider contractually barred from using your data to train its models?
questions.helpText: Consumer tiers often train on your inputs by default and offer no AVV; business/enterprise tiers usually exclude training and include the contract. A training opt-out only covers training, not the AVV.

options.label: Yes, training is excluded by contract
No / training is allowed by default

questions.prompt: Does this AI support a critical or important business function at a regulated firm (e.g. a financial entity under DORA/KAGB)?
questions.helpText: If yes, the provider contract is an outsourcing and must add audit rights, exit/termination, sub-provider transparency and incident reporting (DORA Art. 30).

questions.prompt: Where is the personal data stored or processed?
questions.helpText: Anything other than EU/EEA-only is a restricted international transfer (Chapter V).

questions.prompt: Can anyone outside the EU/EEA access the data (e.g. remote support, an overseas team)?
questions.helpText: Remote access from outside the EEA is itself a transfer, even if the servers are in the EU.

questions.prompt: For any non-US country outside the EEA where the data goes, is it covered by an EU adequacy decision (for example the UK, Switzerland, Canada, Japan, or South Korea)?
questions.helpText: An adequacy decision (Art. 45) means transfers there need no extra safeguard. Without adequacy you need SCCs or another Art. 46 tool.

questions.prompt: For transfers to countries without an adequacy decision or DPF cover, do you have signed EU Standard Contractual Clauses (SCC) or another Art. 46 safeguard in place?
questions.helpText: SCCs are the usual Art. 46 mechanism after Schrems II. They must be the current 2021 EU SCCs and actually signed with the data importer.

questions.prompt: Have you completed a Transfer Impact Assessment (TIA) for those transfers?
questions.helpText: Schrems II requires a case-by-case TIA whenever you rely on SCCs: check the destination country's laws and add supplementary measures (for example encryption) where needed.

questions.prompt: If you use a US provider, is it self-certified under the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework (DPF)?
questions.helpText: Look the provider up on the official list at dataprivacyframework.gov. The DPF is an adequacy decision (Art. 45), so a certified provider means US storage is lawful without SCCs. This is the transfer basis only and does not replace the Art. 28 processor contract (AVV).

options.label: Yes, it is on the DPF list

questions.prompt: Does it involve large-scale or systematic monitoring or profiling of people?
questions.helpText: Systematic monitoring is a common DPIA and DPO trigger.

questions.prompt: Do you use personal data to train, fine-tune or improve the AI model?
questions.helpText: Training on personal data raises purpose-limitation and erasure challenges.

questions.prompt: Do you use special-category data (for example health or ethnic origin) to detect or correct bias in an AI system?
questions.helpText: The AI Act's Art. 4a (added in 2026) allows this only as an exception and with strict safeguards.

questions.prompt: Have you defined how long the data is kept and when it is deleted?
questions.helpText: Personal data must not be kept longer than necessary (Art. 5(1)(e)).

questions.prompt: Do you have a process to detect and report a personal-data breach within 72 hours?
questions.helpText: Breaches must reach the regulator within 72 hours (Art. 33).

questions.prompt: Have you appointed a Data Protection Officer (DPO)?
questions.helpText: Mandatory for large-scale/special-category core activities, or 20+ staff in Germany.

obligations.title: Establish a lawful basis for processing
obligations.lawExplanation: Processing is lawful only if at least one of the six Art. 6 bases applies: consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, or legitimate interests.
obligations.why: Any processing of personal data needs a documented lawful basis before it starts.
obligations.solution: Record the lawful basis for this system and the reasoning behind it.

obligations.title: Meet the conditions for valid consent
obligations.lawExplanation: Consent must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous, separable from other terms, and as easy to withdraw as to give.
obligations.why: You rely on consent, so it must meet the Art. 7 standard or it is invalid.
obligations.solution: Use an unticked, granular opt-in, log when/how consent was given, and offer one-click withdrawal that stops the processing.
obligations.exemptionNote: Consent is generally NOT a valid basis where there is a power imbalance, e.g. between an employer and employees — use a different Art. 6 basis there.

obligations.title: Run a Legitimate Interests Assessment
obligations.lawExplanation: Legitimate interests requires a three-part test: a real interest, that the processing is necessary for it, and that it is not overridden by the individual's rights.
obligations.why: You rely on legitimate interests, which is only valid once the balancing test is passed and recorded.
obligations.solution: Document a Legitimate Interests Assessment (purpose, necessity, balancing) and keep it on file; tell people they can object.
obligations.exemptionNote: This basis is not available to public authorities acting in their official tasks.

obligations.title: Keep a Record of Processing Activities (controller)
obligations.lawExplanation: Controllers must keep a written record of processing: purposes, data categories, recipients, transfers, retention and security measures.
obligations.why: As the controller you must document this system's processing in your RoPA.
obligations.solution: Add this AI system to your RoPA with purpose, data categories, recipients (incl. processors), transfers and retention.
obligations.exemptionNote: Art. 30(5): organisations with fewer than 250 employees are exempt — BUT only if the processing is occasional, not risky, and has no special-category/criminal data. AI processing rarely meets all three, so the exemption usually does not help.

obligations.title: Keep a processor's Record of Processing
obligations.lawExplanation: Processors must record the categories of processing carried out for each controller, plus transfers and security measures.
obligations.why: You act as a processor, so you keep a processor-side record.
obligations.solution: Maintain a record listing each controller, the processing categories, transfers, and your security measures.

obligations.title: Provide a privacy notice
obligations.lawExplanation: You must tell people who you are, why you process their data, the lawful basis, recipients, retention, their rights, and any automated decision-making — at collection (Art. 13) or within one month if obtained indirectly (Art. 14).
obligations.why: People whose data this system uses must be informed about it.
obligations.solution: Ensure your privacy notice covers this system, including AI-specific processing and any automated decisions.

obligations.title: Implement appropriate security measures
obligations.lawExplanation: Technical and organisational measures must match the risk — e.g. encryption, pseudonymisation, access control, and the ability to restore data after an incident.
obligations.why: All personal data must be protected with measures matched to the risk.
obligations.solution: Document encryption in transit/at rest, access control for the AI provider, logging and backups for this system.

obligations.title: Be able to honour data-subject rights
obligations.lawExplanation: People have the right of access, rectification, erasure, restriction, portability and objection. You must respond within one month, extendable by two further months for complex requests.
obligations.why: People can exercise these rights over data held in this system and its processors.
obligations.solution: Confirm you can locate, export, correct and delete a person's data in this system and any processor within one month.

obligations.title: Define retention and deletion
obligations.lawExplanation: Personal data must be kept in identifiable form no longer than necessary for the purpose.
obligations.why: Undefined or unenforced retention breaches the storage-limitation principle.
obligations.solution: Set a retention period and an automatic deletion or review step when it expires.

obligations.title: Have a 72-hour breach process
obligations.lawExplanation: Notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours of becoming aware of a breach (Art. 33); tell affected people without undue delay when the risk to them is high (Art. 34).
obligations.why: You must be able to detect and report breaches involving this system in time.
obligations.solution: Put a breach runbook in place: detection, escalation, a 72-hour authority notification path, and a breach register.
obligations.exemptionNote: Individuals need not be notified if the data was unintelligible to outsiders (e.g. strongly encrypted) or you have since neutralised the risk.

obligations.title: Sign a Data Processing Agreement with each processor
obligations.lawExplanation: A binding written contract is required whenever a processor handles personal data for you, covering the eight Art. 28(3) points: subject matter, duration, instructions, confidentiality, security, sub-processing, assistance, and deletion/return.
obligations.why: You use a third-party processor, so an Art. 28 DPA is legally required.
obligations.solution: Put a signed DPA in place with every processor covering all Art. 28(3) clauses, and keep a copy on file. Note that consumer AI tiers usually offer no DPA; a business or enterprise tier includes the standard DPA automatically. The DPA must also cover audit rights, sub-processor transparency and deletion or return of data at the end. If this AI supports a critical or important function at a regulated firm, DORA Art. 30 (and KAGB outsourcing rules) add further contract requirements: audit rights, exit and termination rights, sub-provider transparency and incident reporting, which usually need an enterprise agreement.

obligations.title: Make sure your AVV covers all Art. 28(3) requirements
obligations.lawExplanation: A Data Processing Agreement is only valid if it contains the eight mandatory Art. 28(3) clauses: documented instructions, confidentiality, security (Art. 32), sub-processor approval, assistance with data-subject requests and breach handling, audit rights, and deletion or return of the data at the end.
obligations.why: You have an AVV in place, but it must actually cover all Art. 28(3) elements to be legally sufficient.
obligations.solution: Review each signed AVV against the eight Art. 28(3) points and add any missing clauses (especially audit rights, sub-processor transparency, and deletion/return of data). Consumer AI tiers rarely include a complete AVV; a business or enterprise tier binds the standard AVV automatically. Keep the signed copy on file.

obligations.title: Bar your AI provider from training on your data
obligations.lawExplanation: A processor may only use your personal data on your documented instructions. Many consumer AI tiers use your inputs to train their models by default and offer no AVV; business and enterprise tiers exclude training by default and include the contract. A training opt-out covers only model training and does not replace the AVV, the shorter retention or audit rights.
obligations.why: You use a third-party AI provider, so its use of your data, including for training, must be controlled by contract.
obligations.solution: Use a business or enterprise tier where training is off by default and an AVV is included, or get a written instruction that the provider will not train on your data. Treat this as additional to, not a substitute for, the Art. 28 AVV.

obligations.title: Meet outsourcing contract requirements for critical functions
obligations.lawExplanation: When an AI service supports a critical or important function at a regulated financial entity, using it is an outsourcing. The contract must go beyond the AVV and grant audit and access rights, exit and termination rights, transparency over sub-providers and incident reporting. These terms are typically only available on an enterprise agreement.
obligations.why: You indicated this AI supports a critical or important function at a regulated firm.
obligations.solution: Put an enterprise-grade outsourcing contract in place that includes audit/access rights, a documented exit strategy, sub-provider transparency and incident-reporting duties, and record the outsourcing in your register. Confirm your DORA assessment of whether the function is critical or important.

obligations.title: Authorise and flow down to sub-processors
obligations.lawExplanation: A processor may only engage sub-processors with the controller's authorisation and must impose the same data-protection terms on them.
obligations.why: Your processor uses sub-processors, so the chain must be authorised and flowed down.
obligations.solution: Keep the sub-processor list, require prior notice of changes with a right to object, and confirm the same terms are flowed down.

obligations.title: Meet your duties as a processor
obligations.lawExplanation: A processor must act only on documented instructions, keep data confidential, help the controller with security, breaches and requests, and delete or return data at the end.
obligations.why: You act as a processor for another organisation.
obligations.solution: Process only on the controller's documented instructions, assist with requests/breaches, and define deletion/return at contract end.

obligations.title: Put a joint-controller arrangement in place
obligations.lawExplanation: Where two parties jointly decide purposes and means, a transparent arrangement must allocate responsibilities, especially for transparency and rights.
obligations.why: You decide purposes jointly with another organisation.
obligations.solution: Agree and document who does what, and make the essence of the arrangement available to data subjects.

obligations.title: Cover international data transfers
obligations.lawExplanation: Storing personal data with a provider outside the EEA is allowed when a transfer safeguard is in place. The simplest is an adequacy decision (Art. 45): for the United States this is the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework (DPF), with further decisions for the UK, Switzerland, Japan and others. Only where no adequacy decision covers the provider do you need Standard Contractual Clauses (Decision 2021/914, Art. 46) plus a transfer impact assessment, or a narrow Art. 49 derogation. This transfer basis is separate from, and additional to, the Art. 28 processor contract (AVV).
obligations.why: Data leaves the EEA or can be accessed from outside it, which is a restricted transfer.
obligations.solution: First check for an adequacy decision. For a US provider, confirm it self-certifies to the Data Privacy Framework on the official list at dataprivacyframework.gov; if it does, the transfer is lawful and you simply document reliance on the adequacy decision (Art. 45 / DPF). Only if no adequacy decision applies do you put the 2021 SCCs in place and complete a Transfer Impact Assessment. Keep this separate from the Art. 28 AVV, which you still need either way.
obligations.exemptionNote: Does NOT apply where everything stays inside the EU/EEA, or the destination has an adequacy decision (e.g. Switzerland, UK, Japan, and US firms under the Data Privacy Framework).

obligations.title: Rely on the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework for US storage
obligations.lawExplanation: Since July 2023 the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework (DPF) is an adequacy decision under Art. 45. If your US provider self-certifies to the DPF, storing and processing personal data with it is lawful and needs no Standard Contractual Clauses. The DPF is the transfer basis only; it does not replace the Art. 28 processor contract (AVV), the shorter retention or the audit rights, which you still need.
obligations.why: You use a US provider, so DPF certification is usually the cleanest lawful basis for storing data there.
obligations.solution: Look up the provider on the official DPF list at dataprivacyframework.gov. If it is certified, document that you rely on the adequacy decision (Art. 45 / DPF) and keep a copy of the listing. If it is not certified, fall back to the 2021 SCCs plus a transfer impact assessment.

obligations.title: Put a transfer safeguard in place (SCCs)
obligations.lawExplanation: Personal data may only leave the EEA to a country without an adequacy decision when an Art. 46 safeguard is in place, most commonly the EU Standard Contractual Clauses (2021), signed with the data importer.
obligations.why: Your data goes to a country outside the EEA that is not covered by an adequacy decision, so a transfer safeguard is required.
obligations.solution: Sign the current 2021 EU Standard Contractual Clauses with the importer for the correct module, or use another Art. 46 tool such as Binding Corporate Rules or an approved code. Keep a signed copy and list the transfer in your records. Where an adequacy decision covers the country, you can rely on that instead.
obligations.exemptionNote: Does NOT apply where the country has an adequacy decision, or a US provider is covered by the Data Privacy Framework.

obligations.title: Run a Transfer Impact Assessment (Schrems II)
obligations.lawExplanation: After the Schrems II ruling, relying on SCCs (or the DPF) is not enough on its own. You must assess whether the destination country's laws undermine the protection and add supplementary measures where they do.
obligations.why: You transfer personal data outside the EEA under SCCs or a similar tool, so a case-by-case Transfer Impact Assessment is required.
obligations.solution: Document a TIA for each third-country transfer: map the data flow, assess the destination's surveillance and access laws, and add supplementary measures (strong encryption with EU-held keys, pseudonymisation, contractual and organisational controls) where the assessment shows a risk. Re-check it periodically.
obligations.exemptionNote: Not needed where the destination has an adequacy decision.

obligations.title: Find a condition for special-category data
obligations.lawExplanation: Processing special-category data is prohibited unless one of the ten Art. 9(2) conditions applies — most often explicit consent or a substantial public interest with a legal basis.
obligations.why: This system processes special-category data, which is prohibited without an Art. 9(2) condition.
obligations.solution: Identify and document the Art. 9(2) condition you rely on. This processing almost always also requires a DPIA.
obligations.exemptionNote: Does NOT apply to data that merely looks sensitive but is not used to infer a protected trait, nor to truly anonymised data. Criminal-offence data is covered separately by Art. 10, not Art. 9.

obligations.title: Meet the safeguards for using sensitive data to detect bias
obligations.lawExplanation: Art. 4a of the AI Act, added by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, lets providers and deployers of AI systems and models process special categories of personal data as an exception, where this is strictly necessary to detect and correct bias. It replaces the former Art. 10(5) and comes with safeguards that must all be met.
obligations.why: Special-category data is the most protected data under the GDPR. Using it for bias testing without the Art. 4a safeguards would be unlawful processing under Art. 9 GDPR.
obligations.solution: Before you use the data, document why other data (including synthetic or anonymised data) cannot achieve the purpose. Pseudonymise it, limit and log who can access it, do not pass it on to anyone else, and delete it once the bias is corrected. Record this in your records of processing.

obligations.title: Handle criminal-offence data lawfully
obligations.lawExplanation: Data on criminal convictions and offences may only be processed under the control of official authority or where authorised by EU/Member-State law with appropriate safeguards.
obligations.why: You indicated the system processes criminal-offence data.
obligations.solution: Confirm a specific legal authorisation for this processing and apply the additional safeguards; do not rely on Art. 9 conditions alone.

obligations.title: Add safeguards for automated decisions
obligations.lawExplanation: Decisions based solely on automated processing with legal or similarly significant effects are restricted; people have the right to human intervention, to express their view, and to contest the decision.
obligations.why: This system makes automated decisions with significant effects on people.
obligations.solution: Provide meaningful human review, allow people to contest outcomes, explain the logic, and confirm a lawful ground for the automated decision.
obligations.exemptionNote: Does NOT apply if a human meaningfully reviews each decision, the effect is not legal/significant, or it is necessary for a contract, authorised by law, or based on explicit consent (with safeguards).

obligations.title: Carry out a Data Protection Impact Assessment
obligations.lawExplanation: A DPIA is required before processing likely to be high-risk — e.g. large-scale special-category data, systematic profiling, or new technologies such as AI.
obligations.why: Your answers indicate high-risk processing (scale, sensitivity, profiling or model training), which triggers a DPIA.
obligations.solution: Complete a DPIA covering the processing, necessity/proportionality, risks and mitigations. Consult your DPO; if high residual risk remains, consult the authority first (Art. 36).
obligations.exemptionNote: Not required where the processing is unlikely to be high-risk, or it appears on the supervisory authority's published 'no-DPIA' list.

obligations.title: Appoint a Data Protection Officer
obligations.lawExplanation: A DPO is required where core activities involve large-scale regular monitoring or large-scale special-category data (Art. 37). Germany goes further: §38 BDSG requires one as soon as 20 or more people are constantly engaged in automated processing.
obligations.why: Your scale, sensitivity, or German headcount threshold (20+) is likely to require a DPO.
obligations.solution: Appoint a DPO (internal or external), publish their contact details, and let them report independently to top management.
obligations.exemptionNote: Not mandatory below these thresholds — but many organisations appoint one voluntarily.

obligations.title: Appoint an EU representative
obligations.lawExplanation: Controllers not established in the EU but offering goods/services to people in the EU must designate, in writing, a representative within the Union.
obligations.why: Your organisation is outside the EU but serves people in the EU.
obligations.solution: Appoint an EU-based representative, name them in your privacy notice, and have them hold a copy of your RoPA.
obligations.exemptionNote: Art. 27(2): not required if processing is occasional, includes no large-scale special-category or criminal data, and is unlikely to risk people's rights.

obligations.title: Apply extra protection for children's data
obligations.lawExplanation: For online services offered to children, consent is only valid if the child is at least the national age threshold — 16 in Germany — otherwise a parent must consent, and you must make reasonable efforts to verify it.
obligations.why: This system processes children's data.
obligations.solution: Use age-appropriate, plain-language notices, verify parental consent under 16, and minimise the data collected from children.

obligations.title: Honour the right to object to marketing
obligations.lawExplanation: Art. 21 gives an absolute right to object to direct marketing. Germany's TDDDG additionally requires prior consent for cookies/tracking and for most electronic marketing.
obligations.why: You use the data for direct marketing or advertising profiling.
obligations.solution: Offer a clear opt-out in every message, stop immediately on objection, and obtain TDDDG consent for any tracking used to profile recipients.

obligations.title: Control personal data used for model training
obligations.lawExplanation: Purpose limitation and data minimisation mean personal data collected for one purpose cannot simply be reused to train a model, and only necessary data may be used.
obligations.why: You use personal data to train or fine-tune the model, raising purpose-limitation, minimisation and erasure issues.
obligations.solution: Confirm a compatible purpose and lawful basis for training, minimise and pseudonymise the training set, and document how you would handle erasure of data already learned by the model.
